---
title: "Binary treatments and interaction effects"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(apexog)
```

## A binary treatment

When the endogenous regressor is itself 0/1, its first stage is a probit and
the average partial effect is a discrete change: the average difference in the
probability of the outcome with the treatment switched on and off. apexog offers
two estimators.

**Control function with a probit first stage** (`firststage = "probit"`; in
Stata `firststage(probit)` or the `i.` prefix, `(i.certified = subsidy)`). The
control function is the generalized residual of the first-stage probit. This is
the estimator of Stata's `cfprobit` with a probit first stage, and apexog
reproduces it exactly, standard error included.

**Recursive bivariate probit** (`firststage = "biprobit"`). The outcome and the
treatment are fitted jointly by maximum likelihood under bivariate normality of
their errors, with the violation as an offset in the outcome equation. There is
no generated regressor, so the standard errors are ordinary maximum-likelihood
ones. The output also reports the estimated error correlation ρ.

A linear first stage is not a third route to a causal estimate. A 0/1
treatment cannot have the normal linear first stage the control-function model
assumes. apexog still fits it (it is the default in R when no first stage is
named, and in Stata when the regressor is written without `i.`), but the result
is a descriptive fitted contrast, and the output says so.

The `certification` data were simulated with jointly normal errors
(correlation 0.5), and the true average effect of certification on the
probability of promotion is about 0.21:

```{r}
data(certification)
cf <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager, endog = certified ~ subsidy,
             data = certification, firststage = "probit",
             gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10, grid = 11, verbose = FALSE)
bp <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager, endog = certified ~ subsidy,
             data = certification, firststage = "biprobit",
             gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10, grid = 11, verbose = FALSE)
rbind(control_function = cbind(cf$baseline[, c("estimate", "se")], confint(cf)),
      bivariate_probit = cbind(bp$baseline[, c("estimate", "se")], confint(bp)))
bp$rho
```

**Which one?** The two rest on different assumptions, and neither set nests the
other (Wooldridge 2014). The control function is consistent under Wooldridge's
sufficiency assumption, that the outcome error depends on the instrument and
the treatment only through the generalized residual. It is only an
approximation when the errors are jointly normal, the model the bivariate
probit assumes. The approximation error grows with the correlation of the
errors. In a large simulation (*N* = 400,000, true effect 0.211) the two-step
estimate was:

| Error correlation | Control function | Bias | Bivariate probit | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.205 | −2.7% | 0.211 | 0.0% |
| 0.5 | 0.186 | −11.6% | 0.210 | −0.4% |
| 0.8 | 0.104 | −50.6% | 0.211 | +0.1% |

So when you maintain joint normality of the outcome and treatment errors, use
the bivariate probit. apexog prints a note whenever a generalized-residual
control function is in use. The same caveat applies to fractional
(`"fprobit"`) and count (`"poisson"`) treatments, for which no exact
alternative is available. The bivariate probit handles one endogenous
regressor and the average partial effect, not interaction effects.

## Interaction effects

In a probit the effect of one regressor depends on the values of all others,
so the interaction of two variables is not read off a coefficient. apexog
targets the average interaction effect (AIE) instead, averaged over the sample
in the style of `ginteff` (Radean 2023). Three cases, detected from the data or
set with `aie_binary` (in Stata with the `c.` and `i.` prefixes in
`target()`):

| Interactors | AIE |
|---|---|
| continuous × continuous | the average cross-partial derivative of the probability |
| continuous × binary | the change in the continuous variable's average slope when the binary one switches from 0 to 1 |
| binary × binary | the average second difference of the probability |

**Interactions of exogenous variables.** `aie = c("x", "w")` with both among
the controls. apexog adds the product `x:w` to the model (or uses it if the
formula already contains it, as in `x * w`).

**An endogenous treatment and a moderator.** When the treatment is endogenous
its product with a moderator is endogenous too, and needs its own instrument:
the product of the instrument and the moderator. Declare the product as a
second endogenous regressor and point `aie` at the pair. apexog then adds the
product of the two control functions to the main probit (`cfprobit`'s
`cfinteract`). In the `promotion` data training pays off more under a
supportive manager:

```{r}
data(promotion)
aie <- apexog(promoted ~ tenure + manager,
              endog = training + training:manager ~ subsidy + subsidy:manager,
              data = promotion, aie = c("training", "manager"),
              aie_binary = c(FALSE, TRUE),
              gmin = -0.05, gmax = 0.05, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
aie
```

The violation is now allowed on both instruments, the subsidy and its product
with `manager`, each within ±0.05. With `aie_binary = c(FALSE, TRUE)` the AIE
is the difference in training's average slope between employees with and
without a supportive manager: 0.051 at *γ* = 0, and between 0.018 and 0.088
over the range. The same model in Stata:

```stata
apexog uci promoted tenure manager ///
    (c.training c.training#c.manager = subsidy c.subsidy#i.manager), ///
    target(c.training#i.manager) gmin(-0.05) gmax(0.05) grid(5)
```

```{.stata-output}
Baseline (gamma = 0):
    AIE(training ## manager) =  0.051042  (SE 0.012024)  [ 0.027475,  0.074609]
...
    AIE(training ## manager) bounds = [ 0.018002,  0.087606]
```

The control functions are held at their observed values when the moderator is
switched, as in `ginteff` after the corresponding probit.

## References

Radean, M. (2023). ginteff: A generalized command for computing interaction
effects. *Stata Journal*, 23(2), 301–335.
<https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X231175253>

Wooldridge, J. M. (2014). Quasi-maximum likelihood estimation and testing for
nonlinear models with endogenous explanatory variables. *Journal of
Econometrics*, 182(1), 226–234. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2014.04.020>
